definition: Software you rent by subscription and use in a browser instead of buying once and installing. You pay for access, and the vendor handles hosting, updates, and security.
why_it_matters: Nearly every product on PlanPrice is SaaS, so the pricing question is never the sticker price, it is the total cost over the years you will use it. Compare subscription totals across two or three years, not month one, and remember that when you stop paying, access ends: your data export plan matters as much as the monthly rate.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Most SaaS vendors are American, and many list prices in USD while billing your Canadian card in USD too. That means the exchange rate and your card's foreign transaction fee, typically around 2.5% on non-CAD purchases, stack on top of the subscription every single month. Before you compare two tools, check for a CAD pricing page or a "billed in CAD" note at checkout; if the checkout says USD, add roughly 2.5% to every quote and expect the total to drift with the exchange rate. Ask sales for a CAD quote in writing, vendors with real Canadian operations can usually produce one.

Then look at the invoice itself. Software bought from outside Canada is taxable here, and the rate depends on your province, 5% GST in Alberta, 13% HST in Ontario, 15% in the Atlantic provinces, 14.975% combined in Quebec, so the tax line can exceed a month of the subscription. If your business is GST/HST registered, you need an invoice that shows the tax separately to claim input tax credits; some US vendors' invoices show no tax line at all. Ask how they handle Canadian sales tax before year one, not at tax time.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team subscribes to a project-management tool at CAD 20 per seat per month. That is 12 × 20 = CAD 240 a month, or CAD 2,880 a year. Add 13% Ontario HST and the real annual cost lands at about CAD 3,254, the tax line alone costs more than two months of the subscription. If the same tool billed in USD instead of CAD, the card's ~2.5% foreign transaction fee would stack roughly CAD 72 on top, every year, for nothing.

definition: A pricing model where you pay per user login, sometimes called per-seat or per-user pricing. Adding a team member raises the bill; removing one lowers it.
why_it_matters: Seat-based pricing punishes growth in headcount, so model the bill at your twelve-month team size, not today's. Watch for seat minimums. Monday.com requires three seats on paid plans, and contrast with unlimited-user models like Xero, where you pay for features instead of logins. Always ask what guests, viewers, and your accountant cost.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Canadian buyers should ask what currency each seat is priced in, and stay alert when the answer differs by tier. Some vendors advertise CAD prices for the base plan but bill add-on seats or premium seats in USD, so your per-seat cost quietly becomes two numbers on one invoice. Ask for a single CAD per-seat figure for every seat type you will buy: full users, managers, and your external accountant, whom some vendors charge as a full seat while others let in free.

Ask how seat changes are billed mid-cycle. Most vendors prorate additions immediately but only credit removals at renewal, which means seasonal or contract staff cost you the full term even if they work two months. If your headcount swings, ask whether the vendor supports true-ups, deprovisioning credits, or a smaller pool of flexible seats, and check whether "view-only" or guest access is genuinely free or simply a seat by another name.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a CRM costs CAD 25 per seat per month. A 12-person team pays 12 × 25 = CAD 300 a month, or CAD 3,600 a year. Hiring three contractors in June and removing them in August still costs 3 × 25 × 12 = CAD 900 for the year if removals only credit at renewal, versus 3 × 25 × 2 = CAD 150 if seats prorate both ways. The removal policy was worth CAD 750.

definition: Plans stacked in levels. Starter, Pro, Enterprise, where each tier unlocks more features, higher limits, or better support. Most B2B software is sold this way.
why_it_matters: The middle tier is engineered to look like the sensible choice, so ignore the framing and map your must-have features to tiers directly. The expensive mistake is buying the top tier for one feature, check whether that feature is available as an add-on, or whether the tier below plus a workaround covers you.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Tier names and prices do not always travel well across the border. Some vendors show Canadian visitors USD pricing by default, check the currency code next to the price, because a bare $ sign is not enough, and the feature set can differ by market: data residency, CAD payment methods, or Canadian tax features sometimes sit only in the top tier. Ask for the Canadian tier sheet in CAD and check which tier holds the Canada-specific features you need, not just the US-marketed headline features.

The expensive mistake on tiered plans is buying a whole tier for one feature. Before you jump, ask whether that feature is sold as an add-on, whether the tier below plus an integration covers it, and whether the vendor will discount the higher tier on an annual CAD commitment. Also ask what happens at renewal: vendors move features between tiers, and a feature you bought the top tier for can slide down to a cheaper tier, or up out of your reach, at the next price change.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team needs an audit-log feature available only on the top tier at CAD 60 per seat per month, versus CAD 30 on the middle tier. The jump costs 12 × 30 = CAD 360 a month, or CAD 4,320 a year, for one feature. If the vendor sells audit logs as a CAD 100-a-month add-on to the middle tier, that is CAD 1,200 a year, a CAD 3,120 saving for the same capability.

definition: Pricing tied to how much you use, transactions processed, emails sent, API calls made, rather than a flat fee. The bill scales with your activity.
why_it_matters: Usage-based pricing is gentle when you are small and can surprise you at scale, so model the bill at three volume levels: today, a good month, and a great month. Compare it against flat-rate alternatives by computing the effective rate, total cost divided by total usage, rather than comparing sticker prices.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Watch how usage is measured and billed in Canada. Metered units priced in USD convert on every invoice, so a bill that moves with your usage also moves with the exchange rate, double volatility on one invoice. Some unit types also cost more in Canada than in the vendor's home market; messaging and phone-based units are classic examples, since Canadian carrier rates differ. Ask for the per-unit price in CAD and whether Canadian usage is rated differently from US usage.

Get the metering rules in writing: when usage is measured, whether it is rounded up per event or per day, how overages bill, and whether you can set a spend cap or alert. Ask which dashboard shows live usage, a vendor that invoices metered usage but will not show you the meter in real time is asking for trust without evidence. Model the bill at today's usage, at double, and at a spike month, and check whether a flat-rate tier becomes cheaper at the high end.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say an email tool charges CAD 0.004 per email. A team sending 50,000 emails a month pays 50,000 × 0.004 = CAD 200 a month. A holiday campaign triples volume to 150,000, so December costs 150,000 × 0.004 = CAD 600, the same tool costs three times more in December than in September. If a flat-rate tier exists at CAD 350 a month for up to 200,000 emails, December alone justifies switching.

definition: A free tier that is genuinely useful, with paid upgrades for power features. The vendor bets you will grow into paying.
why_it_matters: Evaluate a free tier by what it omits, not what it includes: HubSpot's free CRM, Wave's free accounting, Square's free POS software, and Calendly's free single event type are all real starting points. Find the exact trigger that forces the first paid invoice, a contact limit, a second event type, a feature gate, and price year two, not month one.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

The free-to-paid jump is where Canadian buyers get surprised twice: first by the price, then by the currency. Free tiers are currency-free by nature, but the first paid invoice often arrives in USD, ask what the upgrade costs in CAD before you build your workflow on the free tier. Also check whether the free tier's limits are measured in a way that pushes you to upgrade sooner, such as contact or storage caps that count archived records the same as active ones.

Find the exact trigger that forces the first invoice and the exact price on the other side of it. A contact limit, a second user, an extra pipeline, whatever it is, model the month you cross it and price year two from there, not from the free tier. Also ask whether paid features can be bought individually or only as a full plan jump: the cheapest path off free is sometimes an add-on, not the next tier.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a team runs free on a CRM for eight months, then crosses the contact limit and must upgrade at CAD 20 per seat per month for 12 seats, 12 × 20 = CAD 240 a month. Year one of paid use costs CAD 2,880, so the "free" year plus the upgrade makes the true two-year cost CAD 2,880, not zero. Price the crossing, not the free tier.

definition: The choice between paying month-to-month or prepaying a year, usually for a discount. Annual billing trades commitment for a lower effective rate.
why_it_matters: Only take the annual discount after a full cycle on monthly billing, you want proof the tool survives your worst month before you prepay. Seasonal businesses should be especially careful, and always check the cancellation terms: some annual plans refund nothing if you leave in month three.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

For Canadian buyers, annual billing carries a currency dimension that US buyers never face. Prepaying a year in USD locks in both the discount and the exchange-rate risk: if the loonie slides during the year you cannot re-time your payments, and the card's ~2.5% foreign transaction fee hits the whole lump sum at once. If the vendor offers CAD annual billing, take it, the discount stays and the currency risk goes. If they do not, convert the USD annual total (plus the FX fee) and compare it honestly against twelve CAD monthly payments before committing.

Ask how refunds and credits work on annual plans before you prepay. Some vendors refund unused months, some convert them to account credit, and some refund nothing, and a refund issued in USD months later converts back at whatever rate applies then, which can be worse than the original charge. Also ask whether the annual price is guaranteed at renewal or whether the "annual discount" quietly shrinks in year two while the monthly price stays put.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a tool costs CAD 30 a month on monthly billing or CAD 300 a year annually, the annual plan saves CAD 60, about 17%. But if you cancel in month four and the plan refunds nothing, you have paid CAD 300 for four months of use: CAD 75 a month effective, worse than the monthly plan you skipped. The discount was real; the commitment made it expensive.

definition: A one-time charge for setup, data migration, or training when you start. Sometimes waived, sometimes mandatory, sometimes disguised as implementation.
why_it_matters: Add the onboarding fee to the year-one total before comparing vendors, a cheaper monthly rate with a steep setup fee often loses. Ask exactly what the fee covers, whether migration help is included, and whether it can be waived; it frequently can be, but only if you ask before signing.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Onboarding fees are a favourite hiding spot for currency traps. A US vendor may advertise the monthly plan in CAD but quote the setup fee in USD, or run the two through different billing entities, so the one-time charge converts at a worse rate and picks up the ~2.5% card foreign transaction fee on top. Ask for the fee quoted in CAD, fixed in writing, and check that it is charged in the same currency as the subscription; split-currency invoices also make your bookkeeping and input tax credit claims messier than they need to be.

Get the scope in plain line items: data import, workflow configuration, training sessions, and whether anyone travels. Remote onboarding should cost less than on-site work, and if a vendor flies a specialist to your office, travel time and expenses often sit outside the quoted fee entirely. Put the waiver question on the table early, onboarding fees are frequently waived in competitive deals, and the waiver is easiest to win before you have signed, while the vendor still fears losing the deal.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team buys an HR platform at CAD 15 per employee per month, 12 × 15 × 12 = CAD 2,160 a year, plus a one-time onboarding fee of CAD 1,500. Year one costs CAD 3,660, which means the fee is nearly 70% of the first year's subscription. Negotiating that fee down to CAD 500 saves CAD 1,000, which covers almost half of year two. The monthly rate was never the expensive part of this deal.

definition: The length of your commitment and what happens when it ends, many B2B contracts auto-renew for another full term unless you cancel inside a notice window.
why_it_matters: Put the cancellation deadline in your calendar the day you sign, because the auto-renewal notice window is easy to miss and expensive to discover. Check whether renewal pricing is locked or can rise, and prefer vendors whose renewal terms are stated up front over ones you have to ask about twice.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

For Canadian buyers, the renewal clause deserves a currency check. An auto-renewal that reprices in USD exposes you to a year's worth of exchange-rate movement on the day it triggers, ask for the renewal price quoted in CAD, in writing, with the currency named in the contract. Ask for the renewal notice period and the cancellation window in calendar days rather than "before renewal," and put both dates in your calendar the day you sign.

Ask what the vendor can change at renewal without your signature: price, tier features, seat minimums, support level. The strongest contracts cap annual increases at a percentage you can live with and require written notice of any change; the weakest auto-renew "at then-current rates," which is effectively a blank cheque. If the vendor will not cap increases, shorten the term instead of signing a long one, a one-year term with a renewal cap beats a three-year term with none.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team signs a two-year contract at CAD 400 a month with auto-renewal "at then-current rates." At renewal the list price has risen to CAD 500 a month, so year three costs CAD 6,000 instead of CAD 4,800, a CAD 1,200 increase the team never approved. A 5% annual cap would have held year three to about CAD 441 a month instead.

definition: A service-level agreement (SLA) is the vendor's contractual promise about uptime and support response times, plus what you receive if they miss. Standard in infrastructure and payments, rarer in small-business tools.
why_it_matters: When comparing tools your business depends on daily, an SLA turns a marketing uptime claim into a contractual one, but read the remedy, which is usually service credits, not cash, and note the exclusions. For most small-business software the practical comparison is simpler: how fast does support actually answer when something breaks.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Read the SLA's remedy in Canadian terms. Service credits are usually calculated as a percentage of your monthly fee, ask whether that means the CAD amount you paid or the USD list amount, and whether credits arrive as cash, account credit, or extra service months. Check the support-hours clause against your timezone, too: "24/7 support" and "business-hours support" mean very different things when the vendor's business hours are Pacific and you are in Atlantic Canada.

Ask what the SLA excludes, scheduled maintenance, third-party outages, and beta features are standard carve-outs, and the exclusion list is where SLAs go to die. For most small-business tools the SLA matters less than the vendor's actual track record: ask for the last twelve months of uptime figures and how support is reached (phone, chat, email) during an outage. If the SLA only appears on the enterprise tier, weigh whether the tier jump is worth a contractual promise you may never invoke.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team pays CAD 600 a month for a tool with a 99.9% uptime SLA and a 10% service credit for missing it. A four-hour outage in a 730-hour month is 99.45% uptime, below the SLA, so the credit is 10% × 600 = CAD 60. That is the entire contractual value of a half-day outage: CAD 60, against whatever the downtime actually cost the business.

definition: A time-limited period of full or nearly-full access before you pay. The honest way to evaluate software, if you use it properly.
why_it_matters: A trial only works if you trial with real data and real workflows, sample projects flatter every tool. Check whether the trial requires a credit card up front and what happens when it ends: automatic billing, a hard stop, or a downgrade to a free tier. Set a calendar reminder two days before it expires.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Before the trial starts, pin down what happens in Canadian dollars when it ends. Trials often convert at the vendor's US list price in USD, so your first paid invoice arrives with the exchange rate and the ~2.5% card foreign transaction fee baked in. Ask sales for the post-trial plan price in CAD, in writing, valid through the trial period. Also check whether the trial requires a card up front: a card-up-front trial that auto-converts in USD can charge you before you have finished comparing alternatives.

Use the trial to verify the Canadian specifics, not just the features. Connect your CAD bank feed, create a test invoice with GST/HST or QST, and check the tax reports, a tool that cannot handle Canadian tax categories properly will cost you hours every quarter no matter how good the trial felt. Export your test data before the trial ends, too: some tools lock exports behind a paid plan, and you do not want to discover that after building your whole workflow inside.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a 12-person team trials a scheduling tool, loves it, and converts to paid at CAD 12 per seat per month, 12 × 12 = CAD 144 a month, or CAD 1,728 a year. But the trial converted at the USD list price instead, landing at roughly CAD 165 a month after conversion and the card's FX fee, about CAD 250 a year extra for the identical plan. Asking for the CAD price before converting would have caught it.

definition: Moving your existing data, customers, transactions, history, into the new tool. The most underestimated cost in any software switch.
why_it_matters: Ask what migration help is included free versus billed extra, and test the import with a slice of real data during the trial, deduplication and custom-field mapping are where migrations stall. Just as important is the reverse: confirm you can export everything in a standard format before you import anything.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Migration cost shows up differently on Canadian pricing pages. US vendors often call migration "included" while defining the included scope as a basic CSV import, mapping your custom fields, Canadian tax codes, and CAD bank-feed connections is then billed as professional services. Ask for the migration scope in line items and in CAD: how many years of history, how many records, and whether deduplication and custom-field mapping are included or extra.

Currency and tax settings are where Canadian migrations quietly go wrong. Your old system stores amounts in CAD with Canadian tax codes; the new tool has to carry those over, not rebuild them from a US-default chart of accounts. During the trial, migrate one messy real account, duplicates, archived customers, old tax codes, and confirm the tax reports still reconcile. Ask who does the mapping work and what happens if the numbers do not tie out: free rework, or a paid second pass.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a company is quoted CAD 2,000 for "migration assistance" covering 5,000 transactions at CAD 0.40 each. Their books actually hold 18,000 transactions across three years, so the overage is 13,000 × CAD 0.40 = CAD 5,200, making the real migration cost CAD 7,200, not CAD 2,000. The per-record overage rate, buried in the fine print, was the number that mattered.

definition: An API lets software talk to your other tools programmatically; integrations are pre-built connections. Both determine whether the tool fits the stack you already run.
why_it_matters: Check whether API access requires a higher tier, some vendors gate it above the plans most small businesses buy. Then test the two or three integrations you will actually use rather than admiring the app-directory logo wall; a native-feeling connection to your calendar or inbox beats fifty logos.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

In Canada, the API pricing question has a currency angle and a data angle. API overage fees are often billed in USD even when the base plan is CAD, so a busy integration can trigger foreign transaction fees on the overage line, ask for overage pricing in CAD. On the data side, ask where the vendor's API servers and data centres are: if your customer data crosses the border through an integration, that is worth noting in your own privacy thinking, and some Canadian buyers prefer vendors with Canadian data residency.

Price the integrations separately from the plan. "Native integrations" are sometimes free, sometimes paid add-ons, and sometimes free in the vendor's directory but billed by the third party, integration platforms typically charge per task or per month, usually in USD. Ask which of the two or three integrations you will actually use are included, what the paid ones cost in CAD, and whether API rate limits on your tier would throttle a real sync. Test with a real data volume during the trial, not a five-record demo.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say your invoicing tool must sync 4,000 invoices a month through an integration platform at CAD 0.01 per task, 4,000 × 0.01 = CAD 40 a month, or CAD 480 a year, on top of both software subscriptions. If the native integration between the two tools is free but only on the top tier, which costs CAD 60 a month more than your tier, that "free" integration really costs CAD 720 a year.

definition: Whether the vendor bills and operates in your currency, and what happens when it does not. List-price currency and billing currency are different questions.
why_it_matters: For Canadian buyers this is a first-pass filter: FreshBooks, Wave, and QuickBooks bill in CAD, and Shopify bills Canadian merchants in CAD at checkout, while Xero lists in USD. Beyond the sticker, ask how the product handles CAD bank feeds and tax categories, billing in your currency means little if the bookkeeping does not follow.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Ask one question before anything else: what currency actually hits my card? List-price currency, billing currency, and settlement currency are three different things, a vendor can advertise CAD prices, invoice in USD, and settle through a US entity, and only the last one determines your foreign transaction fee. Ask sales to confirm the charge currency in writing, and check a real invoice (or a trial invoice) rather than trusting the pricing page.

Then check the operational side. If the vendor bills in CAD, confirm whether their Canadian entity charges GST/HST or QST and shows it as a separate line, you will need that for input tax credits if you are registered. If they bill in USD, budget the ~2.5% card conversion fee on every invoice and reconcile the CAD amounts on your statements, since the converted total will drift from the invoiced USD total every month. Either way, ask whether you can switch billing currency mid-contract without being repriced.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a tool lists CAD 50 a month but invoices USD 36. At a typical exchange rate that converts to about CAD 49, close to the list price, but the card's ~2.5% foreign transaction fee adds roughly CAD 1.25, so the statement shows about CAD 50.25 each month, drifting with the exchange rate. A buyer comparing it against a true CAD 50-a-month competitor is really comparing about CAD 50.25 (variable) with CAD 50.00 (fixed).

definition: A fee charged on each sale or payment processed, typically a small percentage plus a fixed amount. The core of payment-processor pricing.
why_it_matters: Do not compare the headline rate; compare the effective rate, total fees divided by total volume, computed from a real month of your sales. Flat-rate structures like Square's suit smaller or spikier volume, while interchange-plus suits higher steady volume, and the crossover only shows up in your own numbers.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

In Canada, the per-transaction fee hides a second layer. Interchange and card-brand costs work differently for Canadian merchants, and payments from US or international customers often carry an extra cross-border assessment on top of the headline rate, a flat advertised rate rarely includes it. Ask the processor for your effective rate broken into domestic cards, US and international cards, and debit, and ask specifically about Interac debit, which in Canada is typically a low flat fee per transaction rather than a percentage.

Settlement currency matters as much as the rate. If you invoice in CAD but the processor settles to you in USD, you are paying currency conversion on your own revenue before it reaches your account, on top of the transaction fee. Ask whether settlement is in CAD to a Canadian bank account, what the payout timing is (next-day versus two-day changes your cash flow), and whether chargebacks are billed in the transaction's original currency or converted at the processor's rate.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a store processes CAD 40,000 a month through a flat-rate processor at 2.9% plus CAD 0.30 per transaction, across 800 transactions. The percentage takes 2.9% × 40,000 = CAD 1,160 and the fixed fees add 800 × 0.30 = CAD 240, for CAD 1,400 total, an effective rate of 3.5%, not the advertised 2.9%. If CAD 8,000 of that volume came from US cards at an extra 1% cross-border fee, add another CAD 80. The headline rate was the least informative number on the page.

definition: Grandfathering means existing customers keep their old price when rates rise; a price lock is a contractual guarantee the price will not change for a set period.
why_it_matters: Introductory discounts expire, so the price that matters is the renewal price, get it in writing before you sign. Ask whether the vendor has a history of grandfathering existing customers through increases, and treat a first-year quote as a sales tool, not a promise.
extra_html:
What to watch for in Canadian pricing

Canadian buyers should check which currency the lock is denominated in. A price lock quoted in USD protects you from the vendor's price increases but not from the exchange rate, if the loonie weakens 8%, your CAD cost rises 8% while the "locked" USD price sits perfectly still. The lock worth asking for is a CAD-denominated price for the contract term; get the currency named in the clause, not just the number.

Grandfathering is a pattern, not a promise, so ask for the vendor's actual history: how many price increases in the last three years, and were existing customers grandfathered through each one? Also ask what ends grandfathering, adding seats, changing tiers, or switching from monthly to annual billing can silently reprice you to current rates. If the vendor will not put the renewal price in writing, treat the year-one quote as a sales tool and model year two at the current list price plus a margin.

A concrete example

Illustrative arithmetic, not a real vendor quote: say a vendor locks a plan at CAD 49 a month for two years. In month 25 the lock expires and the plan reprices to CAD 65 a month, a 33% jump. Year three costs CAD 780 instead of CAD 588, a CAD 192 increase on the identical product that the buyer never approved. Anyone who only compared year-one totals never saw it coming.
